overview: Arabana Country lies around Kati Thanda, also known as Lake Eyre, in northern South Australia. Springs, waterholes and the knowledge needed to care for them connect livelihoods, family histories and cultural responsibilities. Arabana people continue to maintain those relationships through community institutions, teaching and work on Country.

periods.title: Pastoral and telegraph stations change local work
periods.summary: At Strangways Springs, pastoral occupation and the telegraph brought new work, goods and restrictions. Archaeological camps preserve evidence of Arabana adaptation within these colonial arrangements.

periods.title: A head ornament enters a museum collection
periods.summary: Walter Baldwin Spencer collected the netted ornament now catalogued as X23554. The collecting date is documented; its maker and separate manufacture date are not established.

periods.title: Mission life at Finniss Springs
periods.summary: A mission established at Finniss Springs in 1939 became a place of family life and schooling. Its closure in 1962 did not end Arabana connections with the area.

periods.title: Native title recognition
periods.summary: The Arabana community records native title recognition in 2012. Its corporation works on land, water and cultural responsibilities arising from continuing relationships with Country.

periods.title: Water knowledge informs research
periods.summary: A jointly authored report developed cultural indicators for water and Country through fieldwork and Arabana participation, bringing community knowledge into environmental assessment.

periods.title: Language knowledge reaches an exhibition
periods.summary: The South Australian Museum worked with communities and language researchers on an exhibition that included Arabana voices, records and teaching resources.

periods.title: A cultural burning trial at the springs
periods.summary: Arabana Elders and Rangers joined partners in a November burning trial intended to control dense reeds and protect salt pipewort at Finniss Springs.

items.text: The 2015 water report describes creeks and waterholes as places for longer stays, fishing and gathering. The value of a water place includes its history and relationships as well as its immediate supply. Meeting, washing and harvesting connect practical needs with remembered journeys and responsibilities.

Soakages can be recognized through soil colour, texture, cracks and vegetation that indicate water below the surface. Elders and parents teach younger people how to recognize and use water places. This is learned knowledge of particular landscapes, not a single technique that can be assumed to work throughout Australia.

The research employed Arabana co-researchers and included field visits. Indicators considered plants, animals, soil, use and pressures on water. Community participation shaped what counted as evidence of environmental condition and why a place mattered.

The corporation’s Kutha work connects water management with Arabana decision-making. Its project account describes partnerships involving Rangers, Elders, conservation volunteers and environmental researchers. Considering the health of plants and animals alongside water conditions helps turn knowledge of Country into practical monitoring and management priorities.

sections.title: What objects and archaeological camps reveal

items.text: The Museums Victoria ornament is a netted form made from hand-spun string. Its catalogue tentatively identifies animal fur and human hair among the fibres. The object records skilled work with flexible materials, but the uncertain identification should remain visible: a museum description is not a laboratory confirmation of every component.

The museum associates the ornament with Arabana people near Lake Eyre and records Spencer’s collecting in 1917. It does not name its maker. Collection history therefore gives one point in the object’s journey, while leaving important questions about manufacture, ownership and use unanswered.

At Strangways Springs, archaeologists identified flaked, thick amethyst glass derived from telegraph battery containers in Arabana camps. Reworking these materials shows people selecting and reshaping new supplies for their own uses. The finds document technological choices in a colonial setting, not simply the passive receipt of imported goods.

Camp S355 contained buttons, pipe fragments, cooking vessels and other household goods. Broken shears may have been reused as knives, although the authors present that interpretation cautiously. Such finds help reconstruct activities around work and home; the presence of purchased goods alone cannot establish the abandonment of Arabana identity.

Colonial employment could be paid in food and clothing rather than cash. Ration distribution also gave outsiders power over access to necessities. Archaeological evidence of new goods must be read alongside these unequal working conditions.

David Moore’s 1959 photograph at Finniss Springs depicts Old Finke Bob and his wife Jessie. The gallery identifies Bob as Southern Arrernte, with an Arabana mother, Kantyara Nhuka. That specific family history matters: a photograph taken on Arabana Country does not make every person in it exclusively Arabana.

The gallery catalogue connects Finniss Springs with Francis Warren and Laura Paralta, an Arabana woman. It describes the mission’s protection of children from removal and its eventual closure amid drought, water shortages and fire. The photograph survives as a record of people within that wider history; the museum print was made in 2000.

The 2022 exhibition Arabana Yanhi! Tanganekald Yan! brought together two distinct language communities. For Arabana, Elders’ knowledge and memories were connected with archival spoken and written records. Artwork and word cards supported teaching. The exhibition’s Tanganekald materials belong to their own language history and should not be relabelled as Arabana evidence.

sections.title: Continuing achievements and care for Country

items.text: Arabana Rangers monitor springs, care for threatened species and address feral animals and weeds. Cultural heritage work and learning from Elders are part of the same program. Training and employment help community members practise this knowledge on Country while developing skills needed for long-term management.

The November 2025 burn targeted excessive reed growth around springs associated with the threatened salt pipewort, Eriocaulon carsonii. Arabana Elders and Rangers participated with partners. The project was a trial intended to protect spring habitat; its announcement does not establish that the plant had already recovered or that every spring needs burning.

The Arabana Aboriginal Corporation represents community responsibilities for land, water and culture. Its public account links those responsibilities to native title recognition and to continuing family connections. These institutions give contemporary form to relationships whose significance extends beyond the dates displayed by a historical map.

ending.text: Arabana people and their relationships with Country continue. Colonial stations, mission closure and changes in work altered community life without bringing it to an end. The map’s 1600 to 1815 interval is a coverage range, not a founding date, disappearance or transfer of Arabana identity to another people.
